display_title: Official Review of Submission21952 by Reviewer uCpa

summary.value: This paper introduces a framework based on SAE to analyze the generalization of LLMs to OOD inputs. The authors first analyze how OOD inputs can lead to unusual features or spurious concepts within the model, which can be observed using SAE tools. They then experimentally demonstrate that typo inputs degrade model performance and that SAE-derived indicators can capture input distribution shifts. Using SAE in the jailbreak scenario, the authors observe a similar distribution shift. Finally, they demonstrate that fine-tuning using SAE-derived indicators improves the model's robustness to typo inputs and jailbreak attacks.

strengths.value:
1. This work is comprehensive. It includes experiments on synthetic tasks, fine-tuning, and application to more realistic jailbreak scenarios, fully demonstrating the authors' claims.
2. At least in my opinion, using the SAE indicators to observe the input distribution shift and fine-tune the model based on that is novel.
3. The results on models of varying sizes and different tasks make their conclusions have certain practical value.

weaknesses.value:
1. Figure references are unclear. Figure 1 and Figure 2 lack necessary references. Figure 4A has an incorrect reference.
2. The conclusions in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 are not surprising. It seems intuitive that typo inputs affect model performance and have a positive correlation.
3. The experimental design in Section 5 is reasonable, but the experiments are conducted on GPT2. Fine-tuning on a larger model, such as llama, can better support the conclusions.

questions.value:
1. Have you tried fine-tuning on a larger model (e.g. llama) to support the conclusions in Section 5, even using LoRA? Plotting a figure similar to Figure 2a before and after fine-tuning would be a good way to support the conclusions.
2. The authors study character-level tokenization, which is not the mainstream tokenization granularity of current LLMs. Will it affect the conclusions of the paper?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful review, and appreciate that they recognize the novelty, comprehensiveness, and practical implications of this work. 

**W1**

Thank you for pointing out these oversights on our part. We have carefully gone through the paper again and corrected the incorrect figure reference, and added references to Figures 1 & 2 where appropriate. We have also updated the Figure 1 caption to better explain our workflow diagram.

**W2**

We agree that the results presented in Section 4.2 (that increased OOD inputs in the form of typos degrade model reasoning performance) may not necessarily appear “surprising” at first. Yet, in parallel with the results in Section 4.1 on the model’s visceral internals (that the LLM’s internal processing latches on to a large number of spurious concepts in OOD inputs), we go beyond the surface observation of model behavior by grounding the generalization performance gap of the LLM in specific mechanisms of the internal model operations. These insights are parameterized and revealed by means of the SAE—thus successfully repurposing these latent-factor decomposition techniques for the goal of OOD detection *within* transformer systems. This enabled mechanistic interpretability insights that show a direct and intuitive link between quantification of OOD internal processing streams (induced in the form of input samples with typos) and degraded quality of output generation (model performance) on a meaningful benchmark task. Indeed, we think it is beneficial to include these results on how typos link to model performance precisely because they confirm reader intuitions. These more self-evident results are a stepping stone to our less obvious final experiment in Section 6 where we frame the problem of jailbreaks through an OOD lens, and show that with SAE-guided fine-tuning, now directly controlling the discovered internal processing mechanisms studied in the earlier sections (such as Section 4.1), we can efficiently improve the LLM’s robustness to these previously successful jailbreak attacks. 

**W3**

A key piece of Section 5 was to ensure that we were testing truly OOD inputs. This type of highly controlled experiment is challenging to guarantee with larger pre-trained models, so we instead pre-trained GPT-2 from scratch on a typo-free training dataset with a character-level tokenizer to fully isolate the OOD effects. However, we understand that performing similar experiments on a larger model would bolster our conclusions. Thus, in response to this reviewer feedback, we have repeated the experiments in Section 5 on pre-trained Llama 3.1 8B, as suggested by the reviewer, where we use a pre-trained SAE to decompose the latent activations of layer 19. We find very similar results on the larger LLM, albeit in this slightly less controlled setting. For instance, the TinyStories samples containing no typos have a mean energy score of 771.8, whereas the same set of samples with 80% of words containing random typos yield a mean energy score of 858.9. We note that there is more overlap with these Llama energy scores than with GPT-2; this is likely due to the much larger and more diverse pre-training corpus used to train Llama 3.1 8B, making these typos “less OOD” compared to our more controlled experiment with GPT-2. We also find that isolating these energy scores into quintile bins and selectively fine-tuning Llama 3.1 8B using LoRA reveals that fine-tuning on “more OOD” (higher quintile) bins allows for slightly better next-token-prediction generalization abilities of the LLM in the face of typos compared with fine-tuning on “easier” samples. This is inline with our results in the more controlled GPT-2 setting, however the gains here are fairly minimal as Llama has already been extensively pre-trained on a similar loss, likely encountering many typos during training. We have added the full details and the new Figures for this experiment to Appendix A.7.

**Q1**

In our updated paper, we have recreated the experiments in Section 5 on Llama 3.1 8B, and we find largely similar results as those in the main text, albeit less stark due the significantly larger pre-training regime of Llama 3.1 8B. See W3 for a full description of this new set of experiments.

comment.value:
**Q2**
 
We only employ character level tokenization for our experiments with GPT-2, while all other experiments in our present work use standard word-piece tokenizers. As alluded to in our response to W3, we use this character level tokenization as a stringent control to ensure that the number of spurious concepts detected by the SAE was not an artifact of alternative tokenizations introduced by the randomly induced typos breaking up word-pieces. Our findings on the larger LLMs with standard tokenizers corroborate those discovered in GPT-2, which shows that our conclusions hold up across different tokenizer strategies (character-level vs. word-level), model sizes, and pre-training datasets.

**Closing**

We thank the reviewer for their helpful suggestions regarding clarity in the main text, and for the suggestion to extend the experiments in Section 5 to Llama 3.1 8B. We are confident that these changes will make for a more readable and impactful paper.

summary.value:
This work focuses on using mechanistic interpretability method to detect OOD data/model jailbreak attempts. 

1. The study proposes using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a mechanistic framework to analyze transformer residual stream activations. It finds that out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, such as subtle typos and adversarial prompts, cause the model to activate a significantly larger number of spurious internal "concepts" compared to in-distribution data.
2. This internal off-manifold activation is directly correlated with degraded external performance. Introducing typos into MMLU benchmark questions caused significant accuracy drops in models ranging from Llama 3.1 8B to GPT-5-thinking-nano .
3. The framework is applied to make models more robust: an SAE-derived "energy score" is used to select the most OOD samples for more efficient fine-tuning, and the method identifies successful jailbreaks as OOD (activating more exclusive features). A targeted LoRA fine-tuning subsequently aligned these internal activations, reducing the jailbreak success rate.

While the paper presents empirically effective results, it lacks a comprehensive scientific framework that explains how these SAE-based methods can be applied by other practitioners and generalized beyond the specific models and data used in the study.

strengths.value:
1. The typo-based experimental design for the toy-problem is well-crafted.
2. SAE-based methods demonstrate their ability to detect out-of-distribution data and identify jailbreak attempts. 
3. The proposed methods for enhancing fine-tuning efficiency and mitigating jailbreaks are highly effective.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper lacks effective guidelines for utilizing raw energy scores or the number of activated concepts to determine if data is out of domain. Instead, it relies solely on simple comparisons. Statistical methods and guidelines, such as the number of standard deviations from the mean, would be more easily applicable.
2. The paper explores the application of SAEs at various network layers, but it lacks sufficient guidelines for selecting a specific layer when applying the method.
3. Limitations are not explicitly mentioned.

questions.value:
1. What are the main limitations of the work?
2. Can you provide guidelines for using the energy score and the number of activated features to identify jailbreaks?
3. Could you please provide your default recommendation for the layer to use when applying your method? Additionally, could you explain the rationale behind this choice?

details_of_ethics_concerns.value: The paper doesn’t provide any information about the use of LLMs for writing. It’s unclear whether all papers must include such statements, but I thought it was worth mentioning. If this isn’t an issue, please disregard this concern.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their valuable feedback, and appreciate that they find our experiments to be well-crafted and operationally effective. We understand that the paper stands to benefit from a more unified and actionable explanation of our proposed framework. 

**W1**

We appreciate the reviewer raising this point. In the paper, we attempted to illustrate the ability of this composite energy score metric to discriminate between ground-truth in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples. Our experiments focused on proving the possibility of using SAE-derived metrics for the purpose of detecting OOD samples, and for targeted fine-tuning to aid LLM generalization. We recognize that “in the wild”, users will not know a priori which samples are OOD, and thus will not be able to perform such direct comparisons. Therefore a “rule” or “threshold” may be useful for the practical application of the methods presented in this paper.

We present two new options for determining the threshold. The first is a simple significance test found by comparing a sample of interest to the pre-computed distribution of energy scores of the training set. We simply z-score the new sample and calculate a p-value indicating how extreme its composite energy score is relative to the training distribution. Samples whose p-values fall below a chosen significance level can be flagged as potential outliers. We perform this significance test for the typo OOD detection on GPT-2 layer 6 energy scores. We find that using various thresholds based on the number of standard deviations of the energy scores away from the in-distribution means, there is an optimal threshold where the largest number of true in-distribution samples and true out-of-distribution samples are classified correctly. This optimal threshold will vary depending on the “types” and “degree” of OOD that the practitioner is investigating. See the table below and the newly added Appendix A.11 for the full results, at a level of 80% of words containing typos.

| Threshold | ID Acc (%) | OOD Acc (%) | Overall Acc (%) |
|-----------|---------------|-------------|-----------------|
| μ + 0.5σ | 70.3 | 100.0 | 85.2 |
| μ + 1.0σ | 85.2 | 100.0 | 92.6 |
| μ + 1.5σ | 93.3 | 100.0 | 96.6 |
| μ + 2.0σ | 97.7 | 99.8 | 98.8 |
| μ + 2.5σ | 99.1 | 98.2 | 98.6 |
| μ + 3.0σ | 99.8 | 88.6 | 94.2 |

The second approach borrows from anomaly detection. We use a one-class support vector machine (SVM), trained on the in-distribution SAE-derived metrics to determine a boundary that separates “inliers” (in-distribution samples) from "anomalies" (OOD samples). We use this to detect successful vs unsuccessful jailbreak prompts. We find that after fitting this one-class SVM, we are able to categorize successful versus unsuccessful jailbreaks using nothing but the number of additional features activated, at a reasonable accuracy. The results are provided below and in Appendix A.11. These two methods provide a practical recipe for using SAEs to probe OOD samples and datasets.

| Unsuccessful JB Acc (%) | Successful JB Acc (%) | Overall Acc (%) |
|----------------------|--------------------|-----------------|
| 68.0 | 67.4 | 67.8 |

We thank the reviewer for suggesting the inclusion of these thresholding strategies. We believe that these additions make the findings in the paper much more readily applicable.

comment.value:
**W2**

We note that for the toy experiments in which we train SAEs from scratch, we do in fact conduct experiments on every single layer (see Appendix A.7). For the larger models, since SAEs can be resource intensive to train, we were limited to the availability of quality pre-trained SAEs, which are typically only available for a select number of layers. This is the case for Llama 3.1 8B. In general however, we adhere to the principles laid out in the literature of parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) [1] and model steering [2][3]: we treat layer choice as a model selection problem. Determining optimal layers is best investigated with a held out validation set. As far as we know there are no principled methods for determining the best layer without explicit evaluation on unseen input examples. In so doing, our workflow chose the ideal transformer layer as an empirical choice. Still, for some practical recommendations, we find that the middle-late layers of the transformer provide the most useful SAEs and the most efficacious fine-tuning. This trend is confirmed more broadly in the SAE literature for a wide variety of use-cases as well [4]. We have added an additional passage to the Methods section that mentions empirical best-layer selection, to address this valuable reviewer feedback:

> Consistent with principles from parameter-efficient fine-tuning and model steering, we treat layer choice as a model-selection problem and recommend the identification of optimal layers using held-out validation data (Han et al., 2024; Turner et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024). In practice, choosing middle-to-late transformer layers accords with broader SAE evidence that these layers provide the most informative features and allow for more effective fine-tuning.

[1] Han, Z., Gao, C., Liu, J., Zhang, J., & Zhang, S. Q. (2024). Parameter-efficient fine-tuning for large models: A comprehensive survey.
[2] Turner, A. M., Thiergart, L., Leech, G., Udell, D., Vazquez, J. J., Mini, U., & MacDiarmid, M. (2023). Steering language models with activation engineering.
[3] Wu, Z., Arora, A., Wang, Z., Geiger, A., Jurafsky, D., Manning, C. D., & Potts, C. (2024). ReFT: Representation finetuning for language models.
[4] Cunningham, H., Ewart, A., Riggs, L., Huben, R., & Sharkey, L. (2023). Sparse autoencoders find highly interpretable features in language models.

**W3**

We note that ICLR does not require an explicit “Limitations” section. However, we agree with the reviewer that the limitations and implications of our approach could be explained in more detail. We would also like to note that the LLM-writing information is not required to be stated in the paper, it is simply a checkbox that is clicked during submission. We have added a dedicated Limitations paragraph as a subsection of our Discussion based on this reviewer feedback:

> The framework presented in this paper leverages the global manifold approximation capabilities of SAEs, and does not rely on specific local features to be consistent or interpretable. Still, we require SAEs to be “well-trained” in accordance with established standards in the mechanistic interpretability community (such as high explained variance and reasonable L1 loss) (Cunningham et al., 2023; Engels et al., 2025b). Poorly trained SAEs would insufficiently map the internal representational space of the LLM, and as such would not accurately reflect the OOD dynamics of this space. Identifying truly OOD inputs for LLMs pre-trained on trillions of diverse tokens is challenging. We aimed to alleviate these concerns by conducting highly controlled experiments with sanitized pre-training datasets, deliberately chosen tokenizers, and models of various sizes. As well, enabling practitioners to identify which samples are likely to be perceived as OOD by an LLM could open the door to the design of more sophisticated adversarial attacks. In this work, we deliberately focus on improving model robustness against such adversarial attacks.

**Closing**

We thank the reviewer for their constructive comments, and we think that the addition of these more practical details will greatly strengthen the paper and allow for these techniques to be more directly applicable.

We thank the reviewer for their prompt reply, and we are pleased that we have successfully resolved their concerns regarding the statistical guidelines for our SAE-derived metrics and a more detailed explanation of the limitations of the work. 

**W2**

Thank you for clarifying this point. We agree that the inter-layer agreement of our method is worth exploring. We understand that providing guidance on which layer to select for OOD analysis using our method would be practically useful. 

We can confirm that no matter which layer we pick, the identification of samples as being in-distribution or out-of-distribution is mostly the same. Therefore, the choice of which LLM layer to focus on should be driven by additional factors such as SAE availability and quality for that layer.

To directly probe this, we employ the z-scoring methodology described in our initial response to W1 independently across the layers of GPT-2 to categorize in-distribution samples (no typos) versus out-of-distribution samples (80% of words containing a single-character typo). After finding an optimal threshold (selected on a held-out test set) based on the z-scores of the energy scores for each layer, we obtain a binary label categorizing each sample as in or out-of-distribution relative to GPT-2’s learned representational manifold for that layer. As a measure of inter-layer agreement of the ID/OOD categorization, we then compute Cohen’s kappa (a measure of agreement for categorical variables) across samples, pairwise for each pair of layers. A kappa coefficient of 1.0 indicates perfect agreement, while -1.0 indicates perfect disagreement. We find that there is a very high level of agreement in classifying which samples are ID/OOD across layers, with neighboring layers displaying the highest degree of agreement with each other:

comment.value:
**Contribution**

We acknowledge the reviewer’s comment on scientific contribution to the literature. We respectfully believe that our work is significant and novel for several reasons, and would like to clarify what we perceive as the core contributions of this work. 

**New OOD detection approach**: First, while the prevailing paradigm in mechanistic interpretability focuses on cataloging individual, semantic features, we shift the locus of analysis to the global representational manifold of the LLM. We demonstrate that aggregate metrics like SAE reconstruction error and sparsity violations (our energy score) provide a robust, initialization-invariant signal for model reliability. To our knowledge this is the first work to frame the (still unsolved) OOD problem from this orthogonal angle of attack and to propose harnessing SAEs as means to resolve it. Indeed, reviewer Se2j indicates that “the problem being investigated is critical” and that “the application of SAE is novel and interesting”.

**New model editing approach**: Second, we move from descriptive microscopy of LLM internals to prescriptive intervention. Rather than merely observing that OOD inputs trigger spurious concepts, we operationalize this insight to perform manifold-informed fine-tuning and more surgical safety alignment to mitigate jailbreaks. This establishes a new framework whereby mechanistic signals directly guide data selection for model hardening, proving that SAEs can drive tangible performance gains in generalization and safety. As reviewer 4cJN states, our “contributions go beyond pointing out issues with LLMs, and show the applicability of SAEs for robustness improvement”.

**New quantitative metric for model confusion**: Third, by validating that OOD perturbations consistently trigger a surge in spurious latent concepts, we provide a domain-agnostic definition of LLM “confusion”. This offers an alternative to identifying specific failure circuits for every new task, offering instead a more universal, architecture-level diagnostic for detecting when a model has drifted off its learned semantic manifold. This work also lays a path for the tractable analysis of OOD behavior in frontier-scale LLMs, something that is notoriously challenging given the diversity of their pre-training data.

comment.value:
These are examples of weaknesses that I believe limit the work's contribution.

**W4:** The manuscript lacks a comparison between the proposed SAE metrics and efficient, established baselines like entropy or distance metrics. While the paper shows that SAE metrics *can* detect OOD samples, it offers no theoretical justification for why sparse autoencoders should be superior for this task. The authors need to determine if the "Energy Score" is distinct from standard model uncertainty. A direct empirical comparison, specifically a correlation analysis between Energy Score and these alternative metrics, is required to justify using SAEs.

**W5:** The framework’s computational overhead requires stronger justification. As noted in the rebuttal, training high-quality SAEs is resource-intensive and often restricted to specific layers. Since standard OOD detection methods are highly efficient, the paper must demonstrate that the marginal utility of the SAE approach outweighs the cost of training or sourcing them.

**W6:** The manifold-informed fine-tuning strategy resembles established curriculum learning techniques that sort data via "difficulty measurers." Existing metrics (e.g., prediction depth, variance, entropy, teacher model loss) may already serve as proxies for "OOD-ness." To claim a distinct contribution, the authors should benchmark the SAE Energy Score against these baselines. It is currently unclear if the SAE provides a novel signal for data selection.

**W7:** The work provides limited mechanistic insight; the findings are largely descriptive. The analysis should explore how SAEs handle samples that are strictly in-distribution but historically "difficult" (e.g., due to reasoning depth or architectural limitations) rather than truly OOD. Differentiating between "off-manifold" and "hard on-manifold" samples is essential to validate the proposed framework.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for allowing us the opportunity to respond to their outstanding conceptual concerns. We have addressed each of their newly articulated critiques by contrasting our method with conventional techniques and providing additional theoretical motivations behind our framework. 

**W4**

We thank the reviewer for raising this point. We did not intend for our work to be a comprehensive survey of OOD detection methods. Rather, we sought to introduce an intuitive yet overlooked property of SAEs, and demonstrate the usefulness of such SAEs for targeted, mechanistically-informed robustness improvements of subject LLMs. Further, “OOD detection” is only a small part of our method. We believe the main theoretical contribution is the insight that aligning SAE-distentangled latent spaces through lightweight and targeted fine-tuning leads to large gains in practical robustness (e.g. mitigating jailbreaks), without sacrificing model capability (e.g. maintaining MMLU performance post-fine-tuning).

Still, we understand that additional comparisons with alternative notions of OOD in the domain of LLMs would better contextualize our work. Therefore we have performed a new comparative analysis between our newly introduced SAE-derived energy score and established methods of measuring model uncertainty: entropy and Mahalanobis distance. We find that there is only weak agreement between the energy score, entropy, and Mahalanobis distance on the same samples (no typo ID samples and 20% & 80% typo OOD samples), as measured using the Pearson correlation coefficient:

Pearson correlation between OOD metrics, same samples (20% typos)
|             |   Energy (ours) |   Entropy |   Mahalanobis |
|:------------|---------:|----------:|--------------:|
| Energy (ours)      |   1.0000 |    0.0863 |       -0.0692 |
| Entropy     |   0.0863 |    1.0000 |        0.0550 |
| Mahalanobis |  -0.0692 |    0.0550 |        1.0000 |

Pearson correlation between OOD metrics, same samples (80% typos)
|             |   Energy (ours) |   Entropy |   Mahalanobis |
|:------------|---------:|----------:|--------------:|
| Energy (ours)      |   1.0000 |    0.4322 |        0.6594 |
| Entropy     |   0.4322 |    1.0000 |        0.3705 |
| Mahalanobis |   0.6594 |    0.3705 |        1.0000 |


These results indicate that the SAE-derived energy score that we introduce in the paper is a largely novel and orthogonal measure of “OOD-ness” of a sample, compared with traditional OOD detection techniques. This is especially apparent with “slightly OOD” samples (20% of words containing a single character typo): our method shows almost no correlation with traditional approaches.

We will add these new results along with additional experimental details to a new section of the Appendix.

comment.value:
**W5**

We agree that the computational requirements to train SAEs are relatively high. However, they are much lower than the computational requirements to train the subject LLM itself, and SAEs are not prohibitive to run after they have been trained. SAEs, like LLMs, are also general-purpose tools, which have been shown to be effective for interpretable feature extraction, circuit tracing, model steering, and in this work, OOD analysis and robustness improvements. Our aim in this work was to extend the marginal utility of SAEs beyond local feature analysis to a global map of the LLM’s internal representational structure.

To explore the added LLM-specific utility of our approach beyond conventional methods, we perform a new analysis where we compare the performance of a linear classifier trained on our energy score, entropy, or Mahalanobis distance on the task of predicting whether a simple is in-distribution or out-of-distribution. The table below shows that the energy score is a stronger indicator of off-distribution samples than entropy, and performs as well better than the Mahalanobis distance, particularly on less obvious OOD samples (e.g. 20% of words containing a typo):

*Classification of ID and OOD samples, OOD = 20% typos (AUC)*

Energy (ours)  : ROC-AUC = **0.8150**

Entropy        : ROC-AUC = 0.5732

Mahalanobis    : ROC-AUC = 0.7617


*Classification of ID and OOD samples, OOD = 80% typos (AUC)*

Energy (ours)  : ROC-AUC = **0.9990** 

Entropy        : ROC-AUC = 0.7841

Mahalanobis    : ROC-AUC = 0.9818

These results give credence to the notion that our SAE-based approach for OOD analysis is a more “LLM-native” strategy than traditional distance-based similarity measures or loss-based model confusion measures. These traditional techniques may have been sufficient for small networks trained on limited, static datasets, but modern LLMs pre-trained on trillions of diverse tokens necessitate a full characterization of their representational manifolds in order to probe their true generalization capabilities, which our SAEs provide. We are transitioning the discussion of OOD generalization from a data-dependent regime (entropy, Mahalanobis distance) to a model-inherent regime. As we state in the Discussion section of the main text:


> Collectively, by bringing to bear SAEs, we reframe the study of distributional shift in transformers,
emphasizing the global structure of the model’s private representation space rather than relationships
among distributions of individual data points.

We will add these new results along with additional experimental details to a new section of the Appendix.

**W6**

Our SAE-informed fine-tuning strategy is indeed similar to curriculum learning. To underscore the utility of our SAE-derived metrics, we show in the paper that these metrics highlight data points that, when used in fine-tuning, yield better LLM generalization than others. We do not claim that our approach is superior to established curriculum learning strategies for all tasks; rather, we assert that our framework is uniquely able to provide useful mechanistically-informed signals for extending LLM generalization while maintaining overall reasoning abilities. This allows our approach to be used for highly targeted model robustness improvements, as in the case of our jailbreaking experiment.

In our responses to W4 and W5, we showed that the energy score does indeed provide a unique signal for labelling data points as ID or OOD, compared with traditional metrics such as entropy or Mahalanobis distance between samples. Extending these findings, as recommended by the reviewer, we perform a new analysis where we compare the curriculum learning performance of our energy score metric, entropy, and the Mahalanobis distance. Analogous to Section 5 in the main paper, we fine-tune our TinyStories-trained GPT-2 model strictly on samples bucketed into decile bins for each metric, and test the subsequent generalization performance of the fine-tuned model on datasets where 80% of words in a sample contain typos. The Mahalanobis distance performs slightly better, but is still not as effective as our SAE-derived energy score for extending the generalization abilities of GPT-2 to the 80% typo-laden dataset. Therefore, while we did not intend for our framework to be used strictly in the context of curriculum learning, we find that our method is at least as effective if not better on the task of broadening LLM generalization abilities as popular alternative sample selection methods. **W7**

We respectfully disagree that our work provides limited mechanistic insight. In fact, several core contributions of our work hinge upon novel mechanistic findings. First, we show that axiomatically off-distribution samples consistently activate a large number of input agnostic concepts.These input agnostic concepts reveal systematic deviations in the transformer’s learnt representation manifold as a useful mechanistic signal indicating the areas in which the LLM fails to generalize. Second, we show that these global representational deviations are associated with significantly degraded LLM performance on core benchmarking tasks such as MMLU. Third, we demonstrate that using the SAE’s approximation of the representational manifold of the LLM, we can align specific concept activations to dramatically increase LLM model robustness to adversarial inputs. Practically, this technique resulted in rendering 90.39% of previously successful jailbreaks ineffective on Llama 3.1 8B, with essentially no drop in general reasoning performance.   

All of the aforementioned findings are reliant on deep mechanistic insights across local and global scales, as illuminated by an SAE. Our goal in this paper was not to investigate specific circuits or individual features within an LLM. Instead, we sought to fully leverage the global properties of the SAE to confront the challenge of LLM generalization from an entirely novel angle.

We understand the reviewer’s point that “hard” in-distribution samples should be distinguished from off-distribution samples. To analyze how our framework handles “hard” in-distribution samples, we computed the correlation between the SAE’s L0 (number of activated semantic concepts) of the MMLU questions evaluated on Llama 3.1 8B and their correctness. The correlation between the two was 0.003, indicating that the L0 does not meaningfully predict per-item correctness. We interpret this as evidence that the L0 and other SAE-derived metrics primarily capture distributional deviation rather than simply task difficulty. We thank the reviewer for pointing out this distinction, and we will incorporate this interesting new finding in the main paper. This result highlights the specificity of our framework for capturing true OOD signal.

summary.value: This paper is a mechanistic study on the ability of LLMs to generalise to OOD, with a specific focus on controllable generation of datapoints and an emphasis on lexical over semantic perturbations. The methodology operates under the manifold hypothesis, which allows for the definition of intuitive metrics to explain robustness. The topic and thesis are not strictly novel: work on transformer robustness, especially to typos, has existed since at least 2020 with the same takeaways. However, this type of work has (surprisingly) not been explored in LLMs. This contribution, added to the robust, systematic approach to experimentation and solutions proposed, makes this paper a strong contribution to the field.

strengths.value:
In my opinion, this paper is very strong. It is thorough, well-written, and has a good, robust, set of experiments. All around, save for a few comments (in 'Weaknesses'), it makes a good contribution to the study of LLM generalisation. Here are a few of the more salient things of this work:
1. A large set of experiments examining the central thesis of the work _without_ overlaps (i.e., a main evaluation and a set of complete ablation studies). 
2. Use of open/closed models with appropriate versioning and disclosures/releases. Also use of non-pretrained and pretrained models alike.
3. Experiments have a rigorous backing and well-defined metrics. In particular, the authors display a good understanding of the behaviours and particularities of SAEs / OOD data generation and use these to their advantage to provide more robust results.
4. Well-written paper, with some minor comments (below). In particular, it clearly states contributions, framing, and limitations.
5. Contributions go beyond pointing out issues with LLMs, and show the applicability of SAEs for robustness improvement, especially on jailbreaks.

weaknesses.value:
I have a few minor comments.

1. Better separate results from discussion. Every experiment (and sub-experiment) has results and then discussion/conclusion attached. However, they become conflated. E.g., L369 is an interpretation of the results from Sec 5 _and_ Sec 4. But Sec 5 already is working on assumptions drawn from the interpretation of the results from Sec 4 (L306 -- 'The results in Section 4 present evidence...'). The (interpretation) of the results from Sec 4 is given in both 4.1 and 4.2. This structure could be misleading and does raise questions on the rigour (i.e., objectivity) of the interpretation of the experiments.
    - This is _especially_ important since the approach to the study of LLMs is a mechanistic analysis. In other words, the work implicitly relies on causal relationships between the hypotheses and the data. Thus, clearly separating what it is observed from what follows (as an interpretation), is necessary to showcase sufficient rigour. 
    - As an example of this: the motivation of Sec 5 follows from Sec 4, but there are likely alternative explanations to the observations from 4.1 and 4.2 (see the questions below).
2. Reproducibility is definitely there, but I would suggest also adding the versions (or dates) for the calls to proprietary LLMs. They tend to be updated quite frequently.
3. Formality of the writing needs to improve in some (very minor!) areas: namely, while English morphology is quite flexible, I would argue that 'robustify' is a bit less formal than desired for a scientific publication. Another example would be L412: the '=' sign inline for text shouldn't be used here (this isn't notes, it is a final, publication-worthy work).
4. Also very minor: it's 'GPT-2', not 'GPT2'. Watch out for the citation in L142

Thank you for the correction. We have replaced all instances of GPT2 with GPT-2.

**Q1**

We agree that MMLU is contaminated. Our aim was to use a widely recognized and relatively straightforward benchmark that contained a variety of different types of questions. We would find it surprising if these LLMs were fully memorizing all of MMLU, since they do still get many questions incorrect (without induced typos). In fact, our motivation for introducing the tightly controlled experiments in Section 4.1 was derived precisely from this point; we wanted to ensure that there were no possible issues of contamination or memorization that may arise from massively pre-trained LLMs. Again, we see Section 4.2 as an extension of Section 4.1, this time using larger, massively pre-trained LLMs. We find that larger models, despite their seemingly better generalization performance, exhibit similar dynamics in the face of OOD samples in the form of typos (more concepts activated, degraded task performance). 

While it is true that these results could be colored by the contamination of the benchmark in the pre-training dataset, we are doubtful that these results are solely due to degraded “string matching”. In Section 4.2, our goal is not to test pure reasoning abilities. Instead, what we are really measuring is the robustness of whatever mechanism the LLM uses to achieve high MMLU accuracy: this is probably some complex mix of direct recall, pattern matching, and genuine reasoning. Hence even in the extreme case that our LLMs had perfectly memorized MMLU, our experiment with small surface form typos would show the fragility of LLM recall ability under slightly OOD inputs, bolstering the results of Section 4.1. We will change the wording in Section 4.2 to be more precise, and avoid references to “reasoning” in areas where this could be misinterpreted:

> Even closed-source frontier models, such as GPT-5-thinking-nano and GPT-4o mini, suffer impaired reasoning performance -> Even closed-source frontier models, such as GPT-5-thinking-nano and GPT-4o mini, suffer impaired benchmark performance

> ...we next assess the impact of OOD elements in input prompts on LLM multi-task reasoning -> ...we next assess the impact of OOD elements in input prompts on LLM multi-task language understanding and recall

> LLMs exhibit surprisingly fragile reasoning -> LLMs exhibit surprisingly fragile comprehension

To fully alleviate this concern, however, we replicate our typo results on Llama 3.1 8B and gpt-4o-mini on the largely uncontaminated MMLU “contamination free” (MMLU-CF) [1] and find very similar results to the results on MMLU: a significant drop in performance after inducing typos and a corresponding increase in semantic concepts activated as a result of these induced typos. See Appendix A.10 for the full figures. Interestingly, while the trends for MMLU and MMLU-CF are quite similar, the absolute drop in performance and the absolute increase in semantic concept activations for MMLU-CF is smaller. This could be because the LLMs simply get more questions wrong initially (i.e. MMLU-CF is a tougher benchmark), but it may also show that the SAE is able to somehow distinguish between recall and pure reasoning regimes, as the reviewer was hinting at. Our work is focused on LLM generalization broadly, and thus covers both of these regimes under the umbrella of OOD, but disentangling these modes of operation within LLMs using SAEs may be an interesting topic for future work. 

[1] Zhao, Q., Huang, Y., Lv, T., Cui, L., Sun, Q., Mao, S., ... & Wei, F. (2025, July). MMLU-CF: A contamination-free multi-task language understanding benchmark

**Closing**

We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful review, and are confident that the structural adjustments to the text and the additional experiments on a less contaminated dataset will make for an even stronger paper.

summary.value: This paper investigates how sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to identify and understand out-of-distribution (OOD) behavior in transformers. The authors showed that OOD inputs (including typos and jailbreak prompts) cause LLMs to generate spurious concepts in their internal representations, which can be detected by sparse autoencoders. They further extended this observation to achieve the following tasks: (1) quantifying distributional shift, (2) designing more efficient fine-tuning by selecting high-value OOD samples, and (3) defending against jailbreak attacks through SAE-informed alignment.

strengths.value:
1. The problem being investigated is critical. Effectiveness within the constraint of OOD has been a long but unresolved problem.

2. The application of SAE is novel and interesting. SAE is used to diagnose OOD behavior in a transformer's interior, which is an extension to traditional OOD detecting method.

3. The empirical study is extensive and convincing. Experiments span over multiple scales, modalities (vision and text), and model levels (toy models to frontier models).

4. The energy score metric is novel and effectively combines reconstruction error and spurious concept activation.

weaknesses.value: The energy score formula could be better motivated before introduction. This metric, also effectively from the empirical lens, seems ad hoc. Additional explanations on this metric would be very much appreciated.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission21952 by Reviewer Se2j

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their comments and appreciate that they find our work to be novel, convincing, and addressing a critical and largely unresolved problem. We have addressed the weaknesses noted by the reviewer below.

**W1**

We thank the reviewer for noting that the energy score may be insufficiently motivated in the main text. Our motivation for introducing this metric was to combine two complementary notions of “informativeness” that we derive from the SAE. 

The first aspect corresponds to the number of semantic concepts (the SAE L0) identified by the SAE in the residual stream activations of a transformer model layer at hand. These concepts are linearly disentangled “directions” in the SAE space that most accurately describe the sample. From an information-theoretic perspective, this SAE-derived metric of “concept count” is reminiscent of the minimum description length of the data. If a sample is out of the ordinary compared to what the LLM is “used to” (that is, if this observation leads to an OOD internal processing stream), then it is likely that the SAE requires more concepts (and potentially more rarely activated concepts) to “explain” this atypical LLM representation.  

The second aspect corresponds to the reconstruction error (mean squared error) between the SAE reconstruction of the sample and its true transformer residual stream representation. Even with recruitment of extra concepts needed to adequately describe the OOD samples, if the sample is too far off the LLM representational manifold compared to in-distribution samples, the SAE (as a linear approximator of this learned LLM representation manifold) will be unable to sufficiently reconstruct the true residual stream activations from the sparse concepts alone.

If a test input requires a higher number of “bits” to encode the residual (bad reconstruction) or many “bits” to explain an atypical latent pattern in the transformer (many/rare features firing), its total description length is large, implying that it is atypical under the training distribution.

We combine these two easily obtained SAE metrics into a single composite metric for OOD, as it is possible that an OOD sample may have a high reconstruction error but a low L0, or a low reconstruction error but a high L0. The energy score formula itself is simply a means to put these two metrics on a comparable scale. The first term $\frac{||\mathbf{x}-D\mathbf{z}||^2_2}{s}$ is normalized to the typical reconstruction error seen in the training set ($s$), while the second term $\sum_{i}z_i\log\frac{1-p_i}{p_i}$ corresponds not only to the raw L0, but also weights the number of concepts fired by the rarity of those concepts being fired across the training set ($p_i$ for concept $i$). We have added a much more extensive explanation to Section 3.5 as a result of these reviewer comments:

We introduce a composite metric (referred to hereafter as "energy score") combining two complementary notions of "OOD informativeness" that we derive from the SAE.

The first aspect corresponds to the number of semantic concepts with non-zero activations in the latent space of the SAE, commonly referred to as the $L_0$. These linearly disentangled directions act as a compact code for the residual stream. When a sample is atypical relative to the model’s training distribution, the SAE tends to recruit more concepts (often ones that rarely activate) to account for this unusual internal pattern, increasing its effective description length. The second aspect is the SAE's reconstruction error: the mean squared gap between the SAE reconstruction and the true residual stream activations. Even if extra concepts are used to describe it, samples far from the LLM's learned representational manifold cannot be well reconstructed by a linear, sparse approximator.

Together, a large concept count and a high reconstruction error indicate that an input requires many “bits” to encode or explain, implying that it is unlikely under the training distribution.

There are 3 possibilities for an input sample to be perceived as off-manifold by the transformer and by extension a well-trained surrogate model SAE: high reconstruction error, a large number of SAE features being required to represent it, or both of these together. Thus, as a composite measure of SAE reconstruction error and $L_0$, we introduce the SAE energy score: 
$F(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{||\mathbf{x}-D\mathbf{z}||\_2^2}{s} +\sum_{i}z_i\log\frac{1-p_i}{p_i}$

Where $s$ is the median reconstruction error of the SAE training set observed after training, $z_i$ are the individual activation strengths of SAE latent feature $i$, and $p_i$ denotes the fraction of times feature $i$ activates on training set examples. These normalizations ensure that both aspects are captured on a similar scale. This metric is a straightforward way to capture both aspects of off-manifold behavior (poor reconstruction and surprising activation of concepts) of OOD data points in one number.

summary.value: The authors aim to analyze the OOD behaviour in language models using sparse autoencoders. For this, they train sparse autoencoders on a trained model and then corrupt the input samples using typos and test the features that gets activated in SAEs. They find that on using such perturbations, several features get activated as compared to using in-distribution samples without corruptions. They further analyze that using these corruptions the MMLU performance of llms is degraded and hypothesize the presence of large number of features getting activated in SAEs being the cause for that. They further fine-tune the models on corrupted input samples and observe that this reduces the activations in SAEs, demonstrating that the larger number of SAE activations are closely related with OOD detection. They further use this to detect jailbreaks in the Llama-3.1 8B model.

strengths.value: * Using SAE to perform OOD detection is an interesting direction. This can help in detecting some adversarial samples as well.

weaknesses.value:
* The experiments performed in this paper define corruptions in the input tokens as OOD samples. However, this is a very small subset of possible OOD samples. Therefore, authors would need to scale up their experiments and evaluations to demonstrate that SAEs can really help with OOD detection. 
* SAEs are known to be less reliable as training them on different samples can lead to extraction of different features [1,2 ]. One way to resolve this issue to some extent could be to train the SAEs on a very large number of samples. However, in these cases as well it might be possible to craft some adversarial attacks which can evade being detected by SAEs.

[1] Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01822)

[2] Analyzing (In)Abilities of SAEs via Formal Languages (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11767)

questions.value: It would be great if the authors can perform more extensive evaluation to demonstrate the robustness of their claims. For example, they can analyze different kinds of OOD samples instead of mere input corruptions. They can include change in format or style of the samples as compared to the ones used for training SAEs.

comment.value:
We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive comments, and appreciate that they found our problem framing and methods of analysis to be of interest. We have addressed each of the reviewer’s outstanding concerns below. 

**W1**

We fully acknowledge that input corruptions in the form of typos do not cover the totality of kinds of OOD inputs that an LLM may encounter. Our aim was to be able to experimentally control the OOD phenomenon as carefully as possible. For an LLM pre-trained on trillions of tokens from diverse sources, it is not an easy task to find input text samples that we can definitively say are “OOD”. For our primary experiments in the paper, we trained GPT-2 from scratch using a character-level tokenizer on a dataset that we knew by construction contains **zero** typos. Therefore, when we purposefully introduced typos, we were certain that the LLM had truly never seen these examples before, and we could more cleanly test the LLM’s ability to generalize to these unseen input perturbations. Typos are a useful form of OOD because changing the percentage of words with typos allows us to experimentally control the “degree of OOD” in a sample, something that is not easy to quantify with changes in style.

We also tested the effect of input corruptions on pre-trained models with wordpiece tokenizers such as GPT-4o-mini and Llama 3.1 8B. Further, we tested another form of “OOD” using jailbreak samples in the present paper. We demonstrated that we can not only use an SAE to identify which specific samples are likely to be OOD (successful jailbreaks), but we can also perform selective SAE-informed fine-tuning to allow the LLM to generalize more effectively to the these previously successful jailbreaks, neutralizing their impact.

Still, we agree with the reviewer that including additional “types of OOD” would strengthen our results and make our conclusions more robust. To this end, we perform additional experiments with GPT-2 where we train the model from scratch on TinyStories and treat the works of Shakespeare and a more modern poetry corpus as different dimensions of OOD. We find very similar results to the typo and jailbreak experiments presented in the original paper: the SAE infers additional extraneous concepts in the activations of Shakespeare and poetry samples in the transformer residual stream, and incurs a higher reconstruction error on those samples. This is reflected in a mean energy score of 527.9 for the training set samples and mean energy scores of 600.4 and 558.0 for the Shakespeare and modern poetry dataset samples respectively. As might be expected, there is more overlap in the distribution of energy scores of the TinyStories and the modern poetry energy scores compared with the TinyStories and Shakespeare energy scores. Intuitively, Shakespeare appears to be farther off-distribution than poetry written in more modern English. We also confirm that these energy scores are informative with regards to fine-tuning: fine-tuning on higher decile energy score bins leads to larger gains in fine-tuning generalization on the Shakespeare and poetry datasets. We have added these new results to the updated Appendix in Section A.9.

comment.value:
**W2**

We agree with the reviewer that SAEs are not perfect tools for interpretability. It is known that identical SAEs trained on identical data can produce non-identical sets of features [1].

Fortunately, our results and conclusions do not rely on specific SAE-identified features. Our research differs from conventional SAE literature in that we treat the SAE as a global manifold approximator rather than a local oracle of specific interpretable features. In fact, we touch on this at the beginning of Section 4.1:

> Recent work has shown that SAEs trained with identical data and hyperparameters but with different weight initializations yield different sets of learned latent features (Leask et al., 2025) (Paulo & Belrose, 2025). However, this view overlooks a crucial distinction: while the individual features are not canonical, the subspace that they collectively span is consistent across different setups (Lan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2016). We sought to leverage this insight to better characterize the drift in transformer representations as inputs move increasingly OOD, using an SAE as a diagnostic lens for approximating the minimum description length that the transformer needs to represent the input.

In particular, we show that macro level metrics such as the SAE reconstruction error of a sample as well as the number of active concepts inferred by the transformer to be present in the sample serve as effective measures of the OOD degree of a sample (Figure 1B, Figure 3). These metrics do not rely in any way on specific interpretable transformer features to be identified reliably by the SAE. Different local minima or differently initialized SAEs may lead to partially incongruent feature sets, but our results and conclusions would remain the same, as we are harnessing the global properties of the SAE. 

As evidence for this claim, we reproduce the results in Figure 3, using SAEs initialized with three different random seeds. We see essentially identical results regardless of the SAE weight initializations. We have added this finding to the appendix, and include a clarification in the updated Discussion section:

Our framework leverages SAEs as stable approximators of LLM representational structure, avoiding reliance on brittle interpretable feature sets.

[1] Leask, P., Bussmann, B., Pearce, M., Bloom, J., Tigges, C., Moubayed, N. A., ... & Nanda, N. (2025). Sparse autoencoders do not find canonical units of analysis.

**Q1**

See W1 for additional evaluations on additional “types of OOD”.

**Closing**

We thank the reviewer for raising these important points; these additional results and clarifications strengthen the robustness and generality of our findings and conclusions.
